earlier_scan.source_named: Glottolog mako1250 refs are only survey/ethnographic (Tupper 2007 endangered-language listing, Fenbury 1971); no descriptive grammar or phonology exists

sources.citation: English Wikipedia, 'Makolkol language' (wikitext, downloaded 2026-09-17).
sources.note: Nothing; stub reporting 'Stebbins (2010) reports it is unattested' and that Rosensteel (1988) contains a 174-word list.

sources.citation: Barlow, Russell. 2025. Some areal loanwords in New Britain, Papua New Guinea. Language & Linguistics in Melanesia 43 (Journal of the Linguistic Society of Papua New Guinea, ISSN 0023-1959). 23 pp. Open PDF at MPG PuRe.
sources.note: Nothing about Makolkol beyond its name in a map caption. Whole text a full-text search for stress/accent: 'Makolkol' 1 hit (extracted textMap 1 caption), 'Mokolkol' 0, stress/tone/tonal/accent 0. Incidentally shows that Lindrud 1980:180 gives stress-marked forms for Kol and Qaqet, i.e. the 1980 SIL survey lists carry stress marks, but no Makolkol form is drawn from it.

sources.citation: Arlo, Joshua. 2016. Indigenous language almost extinct. Loop PNG (Port Moresby: Trend Media), 2 September 2016. Online news report; the Internet Archive capture 2016-11-08.
sources.note: No phonology content. Journalistic sociolinguistic report: of 10-11 Makolkol families 'there are only five people who are pure blood Baining.. intermarriage.. has eroded the speaking of the original language'; 'The Makolkol original language was similar to the Simbali and Mali dialects, and can be understood by the Uramat and Kairak clans'; Qaqet Stewardship Council to recognise the Makolkol as a sixth Baining clan. No words, sounds, stress or tone.
sources.venue: Loop PNG (Port Moresby: Trend Media), 2 September

sources.citation: Stebbins, Tonya N. 2011. Mali (Baining) grammar (Pacific Linguistics 623). Canberra: Pacific Linguistics.
sources.note: Nothing about Makolkol stress; p.1 mentions 'possibly Makolkol (extinct) which is locally understood to have been a mixed language combining Simbali and Nakanai'. Phonology chapter is for Mali only (different glottocode mali1284).

sources.citation: Glottolog 5.x languoid page mako1250 (AES extinct; 0 descriptive refs; refs = Stebbins 2009, Laufer 1966, Ethnologue, Moseley 2010, Tupper 2007, Fenbury 1971).
sources.note: Nothing; no Glottolog's most extensive description (most extensive description) reference.

sources.citation: Stebbins, Tonya N. 2009. The Papuan languages of the Eastern Bismarcks: migration, origins and connections. In Bethwyn Evans (ed.), Discovering history through language: papers in honour of Malcolm Ross (Pacific Linguistics 605), 223-243. Canberra: Pacific Linguistics. DOI 10.15144/PL-605.
sources.note: Nothing on stress. p. 227: 'The inclusion of Makolkol with the Baining languages is problematic as there is no published language data on which to base an assessment.'
sources.venue: Discovering history through language: papers in honour of Malcolm Ross (Pacific Linguistics 605)

sources.citation: Tupper, Ian. 2007. Endangered languages listing: MAKOLKOL [zmh]. Ukarumpa: SIL-PNG. 3 pp.
sources.note: Nothing. Sociolinguistic note only; states the sole language resource is 'Wordlist from Makolkol (174 words): appended to Rosensteel 1988'; 7 fluent speakers of ~35 villagers at Gunapeo in 1988.

sources.citation: Wurm, Stephen A. 2001. Language endangerment in the insular Greater Pacific area, and the New Guinea area in particular. In Pawley, Ross & Tryon (eds), The boy from Bundaberg: Studies in Melanesian linguistics in honour of Tom Dutton (PL 514), 383-397. DOI 10.15144/PL-514.383.
sources.note: Nothing; lists 'Makolkol P 2? ENB (Extinct?)' in an endangerment table.

sources.citation: Wurm, S. A. (ed.). 1975. New Guinea area languages and language study, vol. 1: Papuan languages and the New Guinea linguistic scene (Pacific Linguistics C-38). Canberra: ANU. Chapters read: Laycock, D. C. 1975. 'A hundred years of Papuan linguistic research: Eastern New Guinea area', 43-115; Wurm, S. A. 1975. 'The East Papuan Phylum in general', 783-804.
sources.note: nothing; Wurm pp. 790-791 gives a stock-level phonology paragraph ('medium to comparatively high complexity on the segmental level.. voiceless velar fricatives occur, and initial and other consonant clusters are met with') with no word on stress or tone

sources.citation: Fenbury, David M. 1971. Meeting the Mokolkols, New Britain 1950-51. In K. S. Inglis (ed.), The history of Melanesia (2nd Waigani Seminar), 153-176.
sources.note: First-contact patrol account; could contain a few recorded words but almost certainly no prosodic description.
sources.venue: The history of Melanesia (2nd Waigani Seminar)

sources.citation: Chowning, Ann. 1969. The Austronesian languages of New Britain. In A. Capell, A. Chowning & S. A. Wurm, Papers in linguistics of Melanesia No. 2 (Pacific Linguistics A-21), 17-45. Canberra: Australian National University. DOI 10.15144/PL-A21.17.
sources.note: Nothing; Makolkol is mentioned once as an assumed Baining dialect/language. Whole volume a full-text search for stress/accent (letter-spacing-tolerant) - no other occurrence.

sources.citation: Norton, J. E. (Patrol Officer) & B. N. Teague (Cadet Patrol Officer). 1953. Patrol report, portion of Open Bay hinterland and North Bainings, 31 October - 14 November 1953 (object (a): 'to re-visit the MOKOLKOL area and cement the friendly relations already established by previous patrols'), District Office Rabaul, 19 November 1953, with Appendix A 'MOKOLKOL Village' census, sketch map and covering letters. In: Patrol Reports. East New Britain District, Rabaul, 1953-1955. National Archives of Papua New Guinea, Accession 496, ENB District, Rabaul, vol. 2; digital surrogate UC San Diego Library object bb7919945q, pp. 6-19.
sources.note: Nothing on the language beyond interpretation logistics: 'The woman MANO, our only interpreter.. was our only means of interpreting to the Luluai, MALILI'; 'the woman MANO has not learnt sufficient "pidgin" to be a reliable interpreter'. Appendix A is a census of 21 named persons, not a vocabulary. No word list, no remarks on sounds, stress or tone (PDF text a full-text search for stress/accent; thumbnails of pp. 1-45 inspected; pp. 13-14 read by eye).

sources.citation: Normoyle, C. (Patrol Officer, O.I.C. Pomio Patrol Post). 1952. Kol Patrol Diary (Rabaul - Gaulim - Toriu River - Open Bay - Mokolkol area - Kol, 5 April 1952 ff.), with covering memo 'KOL Patrol Diary - Publication', Pomio, 6 May 1952. In: Patrol Reports. West New Britain District, Gasmata, 1951-1953. National Archives of Papua New Guinea, Accession 496, WNB District, Gasmata, vol. 7; digital surrogate UC San Diego Library object bb0445581c, pp. 112-c.121.
sources.note: Only an affiliation/interpretation remark; no vocabulary; nothing on sounds, stress or tone. Diary pages after p.116 (to c. p.121) are movement narrative (Mokolkol gardens, footprints, hunting camp) per text and thumbnails.

sources.citation: Fienberg [later Fenbury], D. M. 1950-51. Patrol Report No. 4/50-51, Mokolkol Special Patrol (Territory of Papua and New Guinea, District Office Rabaul, DS.1/18/1, 21 November 1950; patrol 2-20 Nov 1950, Open Bay hinterland), with the May 1951 follow-up Mokolkol special patrol report and related correspondence. In: Patrol Reports. East New Britain District, Rabaul, 1950-1953. National Archives of Papua New Guinea, Accession 496, ENB District, Rabaul, vol. 1; digital surrogate UC San Diego Library object bb1162208k, pp. 72-116.
sources.note: No phonology content. Report p.6 sect. 7: 'the District Officer had ascertained that the Kalasea area natives and the Mokolkols spoke more or less the same Baining language.. It was found that the two dialects were derived from the same language, though many differences had crept; Interpretation was therefore clumsy and stumbling, but it was possible for us to achieve communication.' No word list is appended anywhere in the Mokolkol section (all pages inspected).

sources.citation: Stebbins, Tonya N. 2010. The Papuan languages of the Eastern Bismarcks / East New Britain language survey materials (cited via Dunn 2012 as reporting Makolkol 'unattested').
sources.tag: likely states stress; not yet obtained
sources.note: Would confirm in print that no Makolkol data beyond Rosensteel's list exist; low chance of any prosodic information.

sources.citation: Rosensteel, Gary L. 1988. A sociolinguistic survey report on five Baining languages: Kairak, Makolkol, Mali, Simbali and Uramët. Unpublished manuscript, SIL Ukarumpa (with 174-item Makolkol wordlist appended).
sources.tag: likely states stress; not yet obtained
sources.note: The only primary linguistic data ever collected on Makolkol; if the wordlist was transcribed with stress marks it would be the sole possible basis for any stress observation. May be held in the SIL Language & Culture Archives (Ukarumpa/Dallas) as an unpublished survey report.
